etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English perce, from conjugated forms of Old French percier such as (jeo) pierce (“I pierce”), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiō, from Latin pertūsus, past participle of pertundō (“thrust or bore through”), from per- (“through”) + tundō (“beat, pound”). Displaced native Old English þȳrlian (literally “to hole”).

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Theodore and Honoria, from Boccace”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I pierce her open back, or tender side

quote.citation: 1926, A[rthur] [S]tanley Eddington, “Survey of the Problem”, in The Internal Constitution of the Stars, page 1:
quote.text: What appliance can pierce through the outer layers of a star and test the conditions within?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To create a hole in the skin for the purpose of inserting jewelry.
(transitive, figurative) To get to the heart or crux of (a matter).
(transitive, figurative) To penetrate; to affect deeply.

quote.citation: 1715–1720, Homer, translated by Alexander Pope, “Book XI”, in The Iliad of Homer, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintott […], →OCLC:

c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
2022 November 30, Paul Bigland, “Destination Oban: a Sunday in Scotland”, in RAIL, number 971, page 75:
quote.text: The flatness of the landscape facilitates views right across the Firth of Forth to Fife, before the railway begins to pierce the Edinburgh suburbs.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Japanese ピアス (piasu, “pierced earring”), itself from English pierce.
